ui.meta_description: One passage of The Urantia Book for every day of the year, with a meditation and a practice for the day.
ui.og_description: One passage a day, a year-long spiritual journey.
ui.subtitle: One passage a day, a year-long spiritual journey
ui.about_html: The quotations are reproduced word for word from the official translation of The Urantia Book published by Urantia Foundation. The meditations are commentary on each passage and are not part of The Urantia Book itself.

msg: As the Foreword defines, one by one, the various realities that make up a human being, it describes the soul in this way: the soul is not handed to us complete at birth; it is an experiential acquirement. At the very moment a mortal creature chooses to “⟦Q 0:5.10⟧do the will of the Father in heaven,⟦/Q⟧” the indwelling spirit becomes the father and our material mind the mother, and a new reality is conceived. That reality is neither material nor purely spiritual; it is morontial. This is the immortal soul, destined to survive mortal death and begin the long Paradise ascension.

This teaching profoundly reshapes our understanding of who we are. We tend to think of the soul as a fixed possession we already have, but The Urantia Book portrays it as a life that grows day by day. The soul is the joint creation of the Thought Adjuster who indwells us and our own mind. The Adjuster never makes the soul alone; he waits for the choices and co-operation of our mind. The growth of the soul, therefore, cannot be separated from the decisions, great and small, that we make. The soul does not grow by itself as the physical body does; it grows only when the mind responds to the leading of the spirit. So two people may live through the same span of years, and in one the soul grows richly while in the other it scarcely grows at all. Soul growth depends not on age or circumstance but on the quality of our spiritual choices.

The key word here is choice. To choose to do the will of the Father in heaven is not some grand religious ceremony; it is the inner decision, in the midst of daily life, to take the side of what is truer, more beautiful, and more good. Each time we choose to speak honestly, to forgive rather than resent, to serve our neighbor rather than ourselves alone, the Adjuster transcribes that decision into eternal value. The spiritual values so accumulated become the very substance of the morontia soul (see Paper 111).

This truth brings us both great comfort and real responsibility. The comfort lies in knowing that even the most ordinary day holds within it the materials for building eternity. It is not rank or learning but a sincere heart turned toward the Father's will that makes the soul grow. The responsibility lies in knowing that no one can do this growing for us. The Adjuster is always at our side, leading us, but opening the door and co-operating with him is left to our own free will.

There is deep meaning, too, in the Foreword's calling the soul morontial. Morontia is the intermediate reality that bridges the material and the spiritual, and it is linked to the new form of existence we will wear on the mansion worlds after death. The soul now growing here on earth is the very seed of that future life. This life, then, is never a trivial waiting room; it is the precious first school in which the foundations of an eternal career are laid. Not one of the spiritual values we gather here will be lost; all of them will be carried over intact into the next world.

I invite you to look upon this day as the place where your soul is born and grows. When you wake in the morning, and whenever you stand before an important decision, pause for a moment and quietly ask what the Father would have you do. Every small step taken in answer to that question shapes the immortal soul that will survive death. We are already walking the first stretch of the eternal journey.
d001.pr: This evening, write down one moment today when you chose to do the will of the Father in heaven.

msg: In the closing part of the Foreword, the revelators candidly explain how these papers were written. Successive planetary revelations of divine truth invariably embrace the highest spiritual concepts already existing in their time and co-ordinate them anew. And so they took as their basis more than one thousand human concepts left by God-knowing mortals of the past and the present, saying that only where these proved inadequate would they supplement them from their own superior knowledge of the Paradise Deities.

This admission carries deep humility and respect. Revelation does not drop suddenly from heaven, ignoring every human effort; it gathers in the noblest fruits of humanity's long search for truth and weaves them together again under a higher light. It means that the prayers, reflections, and experiences of the countless souls who sought God were never in vain. The Universal Father treasures every sincerely seeking heart, and he makes the fragments of truth they have found a foundation for revelation. The revelators honor the loftiest concepts mankind has already attained, while promising to fill them out with higher knowledge wherever they fall short of containing the truth. This way of working, in which human effort and heavenly light labor together, shows that revelation is itself a kind of partnership.

This passage also teaches us that revelation is evolutionary. Because revelation is given with regard to the level of understanding of those who receive it, no revelation of any single age is final or complete. This is why the revelators speak again and again in the Foreword of the limitations of human language. We should receive this book not as a list of hardened doctrines but as a living guide that leads us on toward greater truth (see Paper 92). One who knows that revelation is evolutionary does not make an absolute of his present understanding; he stands ready to enlarge his thinking gladly whenever a greater light shines. Such openness of mind is the very mark of a lover of truth.

When we hold this teaching up to our own lives, two lessons emerge. The first is an attitude of listening for the truth and beauty found in other traditions and in other people. Just as the revelators themselves honored the best of human thought, we too must learn to recognize the genuine spiritual insight that lies behind unfamiliar expressions. The second is the awareness that our own understanding must also grow. Yesterday's concepts of faith must be widened and deepened by today's experience.

This way of revealing truth resembles the way God deals with us. The Father does not drag us along by force; he begins with the best we already possess and leads us, step by step, to higher ground. The Thought Adjuster, too, takes hold of the noble thoughts and ideals already present in our minds and lifts them to higher spiritual levels. So let us not neglect even the small truth we hold, but make it a stepping-stone toward greater truth. To the one who learns with humility, revelation is always opening anew.

Truth is ever open upward. We who read this book today also stand in that long procession of God-knowing mortals, and the small insights we gain through experience may one day become a light for someone else. When we open this book with a humble, teachable heart and live out the truth we read, revelation at last comes to its fulfillment within us.
d002.pr: Look for one sincere spiritual insight in the words of someone whose faith or views differ from yours, and keep it in your heart.

msg: As Paper 1 introduces the Universal Father, it sets before us at once his supreme command to us: “⟦Q 1:0.6⟧Be you perfect, even as I am perfect.⟦/Q⟧” At first hearing this command sounds like an impossible demand. Yet the text kindly unfolds its true meaning. Mortals cannot hope to be perfect in the infinite sense, but it is entirely possible for us to attain the supernal and divine goal which God has set for us.

The perfection spoken of here is not the power to know all things and do all things. The text plainly says that such perfection may not be universal in the material sense, unlimited in intellectual grasp, or final in spiritual experience. Rather, it is final and complete in divinity of will, perfection of personality motivation, and God-consciousness. In other words, the perfection asked of us is that our hearts and motives be turned wholly toward the Father and that our will to do his will become pure. What is required of us is not divine ability but divine direction. The Father does not ask of us what we cannot do; he asks what we can and ought to do, which is to turn toward him with our whole heart.

This understanding brings great freedom to the life of faith. Many people are tormented by perfectionism and condemn themselves for the smallest mistakes. But what the Father looks upon is not the flawlessness of results but the sincerity of motive. However clumsy we are, however often we stumble, if the direction of our heart is toward the Father, we are already on the path to perfection. And that path stretches from this planet through the mansion worlds and Havona all the way to Paradise (see Paper 14). We need only set out from where we stand now. The Father looks less at where we began than at the direction in which we are walking, and he treasures every step taken in sincerity. Even our mistakes can become material for learning and growth.

The text says that this command ever urges mortal man onward and beckons him inward in that long and fascinating struggle for the attainment of higher spiritual values and true universe meanings. And it calls this search for the God of universes the supreme adventure of the inhabitants of all the worlds. Faith is not a tedious duty but the greatest of adventures. On the road to the Father, the joy of new discovery and growth awaits us every day.

On this journey toward perfection we are not alone. The Universal Father has sent a part of himself, the Thought Adjuster, to dwell in our minds, and the Spirit of Truth and a host of celestial beings assist our ascension. The command to be perfect is also a promise that the Father gives us every means to fulfill it. We can therefore answer this call not in fear but in trust. What God has begun will surely be completed, so long as we co-operate.

Today we can receive perfection not as a burden but as an invitation. Rather than blaming the limits of your abilities, examine your motives honestly and renew your will toward the Father. To be a little more sincere and a little more loving than yesterday: this is the step toward perfection we can take in this world. Step upon step, these will one day bring us to stand before God.
d003.pr: Before you undertake one task today, honestly examine the motive behind it.

msg: Does God really exist? This is a question humanity has wrestled with for ages. The second section of Paper 1, dealing with the reality of God, gives a distinctive answer. Those who know God have experienced the fact of his presence, and such personal experience is the only positive proof of the existence of the living God which one human being can offer to another.

The text says that the existence of God cannot be proved by logic or by scientific experiment. The one way his existence is confirmed is the contact between the God-consciousness of the human mind and the God-presence of the Thought Adjuster who indwells us. The Adjuster is the free gift of the Universal Father; a part of the Father actually lives within our minds. To seek God, then, is not to grope about in a distant heaven but to turn toward the deepest place within ourselves. This contact is deeper and surer than any philosophical argument. Arguments can be refuted, but the experience of knowing God cannot be taken from the one who has it, for it is an inner certainty born where mind and spirit meet.

This teaching turns faith from someone else's story into our own. Doctrine and tradition are valuable guides, but by themselves they cannot replace the experience of knowing God. The peace felt in prayer, the unexpected strength received in hardship, the moments when the heart burned within us before the truth: as such experiences accumulate, we move beyond believing in God to knowing God (see Paper 101). The experience of knowing God does not end in a single dramatic event; it is a relationship that deepens over a lifetime. Just as we come to know a friend better the longer we know him, so the more we commune with the Father day by day, the more deeply we come to know his character. That knowing becomes our testimony.

This passage also teaches us how to share God with others. There is no need to win people over by argument. The life of one who knows God is itself the proof. A person who shows peace instead of fear, love instead of hatred, and hope instead of despair is more persuasive than any argument. Jesus, too, revealed God not only by teaching in words but by a life lived with the Father.

This does not mean that such experience stands opposed to reason. The Urantia Book teaches that science, philosophy, and religion each serve truth in their own place. Science deals with facts, philosophy asks after their meaning, and religion experiences a personal relationship with God. Experienced faith does not disregard reason; rather, it illuminates realms that reason cannot reach. The one who knows God is not one who stops thinking, but one who thinks more deeply and broadly while holding an unshakable certainty at the center of the heart. Such certainty becomes an anchor that steadies us in days of trial.

I invite you to spend today conscious of the presence of the Adjuster within you. Set aside a quiet time, open your heart, and draw near to the Father. You need not expect any special vision or feeling. God-consciousness grows gradually in the sincerely seeking heart, and the experience so gathered leads us to an unshakable assurance.
d004.pr: Recall one past experience in which you felt God's presence, and offer thanks for the peace it brought you.

msg: Paper 2 deals with the nature of God, describing in turn his infinity, his perfection, his justice and mercy, and his love. This passage pinpoints exactly what kind of love God's love is. The love of God is not a sentimental emotion; it is an intelligent and farseeing parental affection. That love functions in unified association with divine wisdom and all the other infinite characteristics of the Universal Father.

The text adds the words “⟦Q 2:5.10⟧God is love, but love is not God.⟦/Q⟧” This distinction is very important. If we mistake love for God himself, we easily slip into a soft sentiment that permits everything in the name of love. But the Father's love is a love that moves together with justice and wisdom. Just as wise parents, for the sake of a child's long-term growth, sometimes wait and sometimes discipline, so God's love works with an eye to our eternal welfare. There is no caprice or favoritism in God's love; his justice and mercy, his wisdom and power, all find harmony within that love. And so we can trust that his love will not waver with circumstance, and we can lean on it with a quiet heart.

This passage points to two great ways in which divine love is shown. Its greatest manifestation to mortal beings is the bestowal of the Thought Adjusters: the Father has sent a part of himself to live within the mind of each of us. And the greatest revelation of that love is the bestowal life of Michael, that is, Jesus, who lived on earth the ideal spiritual life. The indwelling Adjuster individualizes the love of God to each human soul, and the life of Jesus shows how that love can be lived in human form (see Paper 188). The Adjuster lets us experience God's love not as a vague cosmic principle but as a personal love directed toward each of us. The Father not only loves humanity as a whole but knows each of us by name and loves us one by one. This is the deepest comfort of our existence.

This teaching also changes the way we face suffering. When prayers are not answered at once, or what we hoped for does not come to pass, we are quick to doubt God's love. Yet the Father's farseeing love weighs eternal benefits we cannot now see. Trust grows not when we understand everything, but when we lean on his wise love even when we do not understand.

When we meditate deeply on the life of Jesus, the shape of this wise love becomes clear. He warmly welcomed sinners, yet he did not leave them in their sin; he loved his apostles deeply, yet he plainly pointed out their mistakes. He healed the sick while awakening their faith, and he fed the multitudes while pointing beyond perishable food to the bread of life. True love thus weighs both the present needs and the eternal needs of another. As we follow the way of Jesus, our love too grows little by little to resemble the Father's.

We too must learn wise love, after the likeness of the Father's love. Giving people everything they want is not always love. More often, deeper love means being patient and speaking the truth, with an eye to the person's real growth and eternal good. I invite you to look today upon the people you meet with the eyes with which the Father sees them.
d005.pr: Today, think deeply about what wise love would mean for the true growth of someone close to you.

d006.t: Love Born of Truth, Beauty, Goodness
msg: The last section of Paper 2 deals with divine truth and beauty, showing how these, together with goodness, are woven into one. This passage sums up the heart of it concisely: truth is coherent, beauty attractive, goodness stabilizing. And when these values of that which is real are co-ordinated in personality experience, the result is a high order of love conditioned by wisdom and qualified by loyalty.

Here we learn that truth, beauty, and goodness are not separate virtues. Holding to truth alone, we easily grow cold and severe; pursuing beauty alone, we easily stop at outward appearances; championing goodness alone, we may fall into undiscerning sentimentality. But when the three are balanced within one personality, that person comes to love wisely and to love faithfully. This is how the divine character is reflected in a human being. Truth binds our thoughts together and makes them coherent, beauty draws our hearts toward higher things, and goodness holds our lives steady. Only when the three values are present together does personality gain its full balance.

The text says that the real purpose of all universe education is to effect the better co-ordination of the isolated child of the worlds with the larger realities of his expanding experience. We live on a planet isolated as a consequence of rebellion, yet through education and experience we come into ever greater harmony with the wider realities of the universe. Learning is not merely the piling up of knowledge; it is the process of attuning our being to the truth, beauty, and goodness of the universe (see Paper 56). Beauty, too, is no mere ornament but a window through which God's character is revealed. In the order and harmony of nature, the nobility of good deeds, and the clarity of truth, we behold divine beauty. Cultivating the eyes to recognize it is also part of spiritual growth.

This truth invites us to check the balance of our daily lives. We should ask ourselves whether we are speaking the truth without love, whether in enjoying beauty we are connecting it to higher meaning, and whether in doing good we are doing it wisely. When any one of the three values is overdone or lacking, our love becomes distorted. When they are in harmony, on the other hand, our lives give others stability, attraction, and trust.

The one who helps us experience these three values in harmony is the Thought Adjuster within us. The Adjuster continually leads our minds to discern truth, recognize beauty, and choose goodness. And the values so experienced are preserved in the soul as eternal realities. A life that seeks truth, beauty, and goodness is in the end a life that seeks God, and those who seek God naturally come to love truth, beauty, and goodness along the way. Love refined by wisdom and loyalty is the fruit of all such seeking.

Reality is finite on the human level, infinite and eternal on the higher and divine levels. The small truths, small beauties, and small goodnesses we meet today are all reflections of that infinite reality. As we recognize them with care and weave them together harmoniously in our lives, we learn, little by little, a love conditioned by wisdom and qualified by loyalty.
d006.pr: Today, choose whichever of truth, beauty, and goodness is most lacking in your life, and put it into practice.

msg: Paper 3, dealing with the attributes of God, speaks first of his everywhereness, his omnipresence. Yet this passage does not describe God's omnipresence merely as an abstract quality pervading universal space. It says that the creature not only exists in God, but God also lives in the creature. And gathering the testimonies of those who knew God in many ages and many traditions, it affirms again and again the truth that the Father has given us his spirit, and that this spirit is man's inseparable companion.

Among these quotations one saying especially touches the heart: “⟦Q 3:1.4⟧Man goes forth searching for a friend while that very friend lives within his own heart.⟦/Q⟧” We strive to find God far away. We are inclined to think we can meet him only through some special place, special experience, or special person. Yet in the nearest place of all, the deepest place of our own hearts, the Father's spirit already lives. The journey of seeking God is, before it is any outward voyage, a journey of returning within. He is already here before we call, and even in the moments when we forget him, he does not forget us. To seek God is really to recognize the One who has already come seeking us. When we close our eyes and quiet our hearts, that presence becomes all the clearer.

This indwelling spirit is the Thought Adjuster. The Adjuster is a gift from the Paradise Father; he comes to our minds at about the time we make our first moral choice and stays with us all our lives (see Paper 108). The Adjuster is not a watchman who condemns us but a companion and guide who leads us toward our eternal destiny. Whatever our situation and however much we have failed, that spirit does not leave us but patiently shows us the higher way.

This truth is the deepest answer to loneliness and fear. Even in moments when we feel misunderstood and abandoned by others, we are never alone. The Father is always with us. One who truly realizes this does not lose his inner center even when circumstances are shaken. The assurance that God lives within us gives a security firmer than any outward guarantee. The Adjuster takes hold of every noble thought and ideal of our minds and transforms them into eternal values. The truth that God lives within us is therefore not only a comfort but also a living power that reshapes us day by day.

This truth also changes how we treat others. If the Father's spirit lives within me, the same Father's spirit lives within my neighbor. Even if he does not yet know it, or does not follow that spirit's leading, he is an honored being in whom God himself has come to dwell. This realization makes us humble and leads us to respect all people as brothers and sisters.

I invite you today to live conscious of the God within you rather than searching for him afar. Even in the midst of a busy day, pause for a moment and speak to the Father in your heart. The Adjuster responds to our smallest attention, and in every quiet moment he leads us into deeper God-consciousness. Our closest friend is already within us.
d007.pr: Three times today, pause briefly, become aware of the Father's spirit within you, and offer him a short greeting.

d008.t: The Meaning of Freedom and Error
msg: The fifth section of Paper 3, dealing with the Father's supreme rule, explains why difficulties, uncertainties, and the possibility of evil are permitted on the evolving worlds. This passage is something like the conclusion of that explanation. Throughout the universe every unit is regarded as a part of the whole, and the survival of the part depends on co-operation with the plan and purpose of the whole, that is, on the wholehearted desire and perfect willingness to do the Father's divine will.

The text then gives a very important insight: the only evolutionary world without error would be a world without free intelligence. In Havona there are a billion perfect worlds with their perfect inhabitants, but evolving man must be fallible if he is to be free. Free and inexperienced intelligence cannot possibly at first be uniformly wise. The possibility of error is the price of freedom, and freedom is the precondition of personal growth and true love. Had God removed every possibility of error, we would have been safe but unfree, beings unable even to choose love. The Father has given us freedom even at the cost of risk. It is an expression of his deep trust in us.

Here the text clearly distinguishes between error and sin. The possibility of mistaken judgment, of evil, becomes sin only when the human will consciously endorses and knowingly embraces a deliberate immoral judgment. Wrongs done in ignorance and mistakes born of immaturity are not sin. Sin is the attitude of a will that knowingly chooses to go against the Father's will (see Paper 67). This distinction frees us from excessive guilt while making us take seriously the weight of conscious choice.

This teaching changes how we deal with our own mistakes. We feel ashamed of our mistakes and try to hide them, but the Father sees them as material for growth. Learning from our falls, correcting our wrong judgments, and becoming a little wiser each time: this is the path of an evolving being. The experience of ascending from imperfection to perfection, which the perfect beings of Havona can never taste, is a privilege given to us. Wisdom gained through experience has a depth that wisdom given from the beginning does not. Only one who has fallen can truly understand another who falls, and only one who has passed through darkness knows how precious the light is. Even our mistakes, in the Father's hands, become resources for serving others.

At the same time, we must be generous toward the mistakes of others. They too are immature beings endowed with free intelligence, still learning. When we understand and help them rather than condemn them, we become parts that co-operate with the plan of the whole. The universe is designed so that each part supports the others as all move together toward the Father's purpose.

Do not be afraid of mistakes today, but be honest in the face of them. The courage to acknowledge and correct a wrong once we recognize it brings our will into line with the Father's will. The survival of the part depends on a sincere desire to co-operate with the whole. It is all right not to be flawless. Never letting go of the wholehearted desire to do the Father's will is all that is asked of us.
d008.pr: Recall one recent mistake, write down what you learned from it, and if any part of it can be set right, set it right today.

msg: Paper 4 deals with the Universal Father's relation to the universe. In its first section the revelator corrects human misunderstandings of providence and asks: “⟦Q 4:1.2⟧Can you not advance in your concept of God's dealing with man to that level where you recognize that the watchword of the universe is progress?⟦/Q⟧” Through long ages the human race has struggled to reach its present position, and throughout all these millenniums Providence has been working out the plan of progressive evolution.

Many people think of providence only as God's miraculous intervention on behalf of particular individuals. So when things go their way they call it providence, and when hardship comes they conclude that God has turned his back on them. But this passage invites us to see providence far more broadly and deeply. God's providence works beyond the passing convenience of individuals, within a plan of progress that steadily leads both humanity as a whole and each person to higher levels. Providence looks not merely at immediate results but at the direction of growth over long spans of time. The life of one person, the history of a nation, the evolution of a planet: all lie within that wide plan. And within that plan, every small effort of ours also gains meaning.

The text says that the two thoughts, providence and evolution, are not opposed in practice, only in man's mistaken concepts. Divine providence is never arrayed in opposition to true human progress, either temporal or spiritual. God's choice of the slow and patient method of evolution is the wisdom of love, which lets creatures grow through their own choices and efforts and possess that growth as their own (see Paper 118). Evolution is not a blind process rolling along without God; it is the way his purpose unfolds in time. Within it we are at once creatures and co-workers.

This perspective changes the way we look at our lives. Growth that seems slow and frustrating, recurring trials, and the long process of learning are all part of the great plan of progress. God does not make us finished beings all at once; he lets us grow step by step through experience. Today's difficulty becomes tomorrow's wisdom, and today's struggle becomes tomorrow's strength. Those who believe in progress do not lose hope even in the face of failure. Just as a seed does not become a tree in an instant, so the soul does not mature overnight. As the farmer trusts the order of the seasons and waits, so must we trust God's timing. Only when we lay down our impatience can we truly enjoy the gladness of progress.

We should also take deeply to heart the words that providence is always consistent with the unchanging and perfect nature of the supreme Lawmaker. God is not one who capriciously changes the rules; he works within faithful and consistent laws. Rather than pleading with God for special exceptions, then, we must learn to bring our lives into line with his wise order. This is the mature faith that co-operates with providence.

I invite you today to give thanks for the small progress in your life. If you have become a little more patient, a little more understanding, and a little more loving than you were a year ago, that is the very fruit of providence. Those who believe that the watchword of the universe is progress take today's step faithfully, even on days when the going seems slow. God is at work in every one of those steps.
d009.pr: Find one way in which your character has grown, however slightly, over the past year, and thank God for it.

msg: The fourth section of Paper 4 deals with God's self-realization, the truth that God is absolutely self-determined. And at the close of that profound theological discussion, it suddenly descends into our everyday lives. The consciousness of a victorious human life on earth, it says, is born of that creature faith which dares to challenge each recurring episode of existence when confronted with the awful spectacle of human limitations. That faith makes this declaration: “⟦Q 4:4.9⟧Even if I cannot do this, there lives in me one who can and will do it.⟦/Q⟧”

This declaration does not deny human limitations. On the contrary, it acknowledges them honestly. There are many things we cannot do. Before illness, before loss, before the weaknesses of our own character, we feel powerless. Yet the victorious life begins not by hiding that powerlessness but by trusting the greater One within us. The one who lives in us is a part of the Father-Absolute of the universe of universes, the Thought Adjuster. The Adjuster, an actual fragment of the Universal Father, dwells in our minds and helps us draw up wisdom, courage, and patience before what we cannot bear alone. Faith, then, is not vague optimism but trust in a real and divine companion.

We should note that this faith is not a single decision but a declaration repeated in each recurring episode of existence. The victorious life is not completed suddenly one day; it grows as, day by day and moment by moment, we choose faith anew in the face of fear. Before the worries of the morning, the conflicts of midday, and the anxieties of the night, we can make this confession again. Confessions so accumulated become an unshakable spiritual constitution.

The victory spoken of here is different from worldly success. Victory is not that everything turns out well, but that we do not lose our inner peace and purpose whatever comes. By the world's standards Jesus was defeated on the cross, yet by his unwavering trust in the Father he overcame the world (see Paper 188). This is the meaning of the words “⟦Q 4:4.9⟧the victory which overcomes the world, even your faith.⟦/Q⟧” Victory is not a life without suffering but a life that holds fast to meaning and purpose in the midst of suffering. Those who live such a life are not tossed about by circumstances; instead they turn circumstances into opportunities for spiritual growth. This is the true power of faith.

This truth heals both the pride that overrates its own abilities and the despair that belittles itself. Those who believe they can do everything by their own strength eventually hit their limits and collapse, and those who believe they can do nothing never even try. But those who trust the God within are both humble and courageous: humble because they know their own smallness, and courageous because they know the greatness of the One who is with them.

If there is something today too hard for you to bear by your own strength, I invite you to make this confession before it: I cannot, but the One within me can. In that trust, begin with the small thing you are able to do. Faith is not magic that does everything for us; it is a living power that enables us, in co-operation with God, to go beyond our limitations.
d010.pr: Before something that feels overwhelming today, confess that the One within you can do it, and take a small first step.

msg: Paper 5 deals with God's relation to the individual, and in its third section it explains what true worship is. This passage delicately describes how the worship experience comes about. Worship consists in the sublime attempt of the Thought Adjuster to communicate to the divine Father the inexpressible longings and the unutterable aspirations of the human soul. For the soul is the conjoint creation of our God-seeking mind and the God-revealing Adjuster.

This description tells us that worship is not our act alone. The mortal mind consents to worship; the immortal soul craves and initiates it; and the Adjuster conducts that worship on behalf of mind and soul. Even the deep yearnings we cannot put into words, the Adjuster understands and lifts up to the Father. Worship therefore does not require eloquent words or fixed forms. Simply turning toward the Father with a sincere heart is enough for worship to begin. We need not be discouraged when our prayers are clumsy and our thoughts scattered. The Adjuster reads the sincere heart hidden behind our poor words and refines it into worship fit for the Father to receive. Worship depends not on our ability but on our sincerity.

The text distinguishes worship from prayer. Earlier in the same section the revelator says that worship is for its own sake, while prayer embodies an element of self- or creature-interest. Worship is a pure response offered not to gain anything, but because God is God, because of his love, beauty, and goodness. In the moment we behold God with thanksgiving, reverence, and love, we rejoice in him for himself more than in what we have received (see Paper 143).

At the close of this passage the revelator says that true worship becomes an experience realized on four cosmic levels: the intellectual, the morontial, the spiritual, and the personal. Worship is the experience in which mind, soul, and spirit are unified in personality. So one who truly worships experiences the scattered self gathering together again and the inner life settling into quiet order. Worship not only draws us near to God; it also makes us whole. A personality so unified is less shaken amid the affairs of the day. Through worship the mind grows clear, the soul grows, and the leading of the spirit becomes plainer. Worship, then, is not something remote from daily life; it is the center that sets daily life aright.

In the busy lives of modern people, worship is easily the first thing to be crowded out. Yet Jesus, even in the busiest seasons of his ministry, kept times of withdrawing alone to commune with the Father. Worship is not a luxury of escape from work but the source from which we regain the strength and direction to carry our work. The worshiping soul does not grow weary; with strength drawn from the Father's presence it goes out again to serve its neighbors.

I invite you today to set aside a few minutes in which you ask for nothing and simply behold God. It is all right if no words come. The Adjuster conveys the longing of our souls to the Father. That time of sitting quietly, remembering the Father's love and giving thanks, makes our souls grow and binds our personalities into one.
d011.pr: Today, spend five minutes asking for nothing, simply contemplating God's goodness and giving thanks.

msg: The fifth section of Paper 5 deals with God-consciousness and explains the relationship of morality, religion, and spiritual experience. This passage conveys the most solemn and yet most hopeful truth of all. Eternal survival of personality is wholly dependent on the choosing of the mortal mind, whose decisions determine the survival potential of the immortal soul. When the mind believes God and the soul knows God, and when, with the fostering Adjuster, they all desire God, then is survival assured.

The solemnity of this truth lies in its depending on our choice. God forces eternal life on no one. Eternal survival is not given automatically; it is attained through our sincere choice of God. Even though the Adjuster is within us and every condition for the soul's growth is provided, the final decision is left to our free will. This is the dignity of personality and at the same time its responsibility. Each time we open our hearts to God, the soul grows and the potential for survival becomes more certain. Conversely, if we consciously and finally reject God, no favorable conditions can save the soul. Our choices thus carry the weight of eternity.

But the true light of this passage lies in the sentence that follows. Limitations of intellect, curtailment of education, deprivation of culture, impoverishment of social status, even inferiority of moral standards resulting from such disadvantages, cannot invalidate the presence of the divine spirit in believing individuals. Survival does not depend on learning, culture, or status. Even the poorest and least educated person who longs for God with a sincere heart is on the path of eternal life.

This is a wonderful revelation of God's impartiality. The world judges people by ability and background, but the Father looks at the sincerity of the heart. Jesus, too, taught that those with the hearts of little children, rather than the wise and clever, enter the kingdom of heaven (see Paper 137). The indwelling of the Mystery Monitor, the Adjuster, insures to every person the possibility of soul growth and survival. No one is excluded from eternity because of where he started. The kingdom of God is not a kingdom of achievers but of sincere seekers. It is not those who have much who are favored; it is those who honestly long who are near. This is great news of hope for all who are cast aside by the world.

This teaching humbles our way of judging others. We cannot pronounce on anyone's spiritual condition from outward culture or moral polish alone. In the depths of the heart of someone who seems rough and awkward, a sincere longing for God may be burning. We do not see all that God sees. We must therefore respect the soul that may be growing in every person.

I invite you today to renew your own choice. Quietly ask yourself: Does my mind believe God? Is my soul coming to know God? Do I truly desire God? For the one who answers these questions with a sincere yes, survival is assured. Eternity begins not in some distant future but in today's choices.
d012.pr: This morning and evening, say aloud your confession that you long for God with all your mind and soul.

msg: Paper 6 introduces the Eternal Son, and in its third section it explains the Son's ministry of the Father's love. This passage opens with a very short sentence: “⟦Q 6:3.5⟧God is love, the Son is mercy.⟦/Q⟧” And it defines mercy this way: mercy is applied love, the Father's love in action in the person of his Eternal Son. If love is an attitude of the heart, mercy is that love reaching out its hand in concrete situations.

This definition deepens our understanding of love. Love is not complete if it remains only a feeling. When love meets another's weakness, failure, and pain, it must turn into mercy. It is easy to love someone who appears worthy of love. But to keep our hearts open toward someone even when he has done wrong or revealed his shortcomings, and to reach out a helping hand, that is applied love, that is mercy. The Eternal Son is the personal expression of just such love.

Drawing on how love is comprehended on a sex planet, the text says that the love of God is more comparable to the love of a father, while the love of the Eternal Son is more like the affection of a mother. The revelator himself admits that such illustrations are crude, but uses them to convey that there is a difference, not in divine content but in quality and technique of expression. If the Father's love is a love that establishes and leads us, the Son's love is a love that embraces us and soothes our wounds. The two loves are one, yet they come to us in different textures. When we draw near to God, the face we meet is not that of a stern judge but a merciful face that understands our circumstances.

This truth gives us great courage in approaching God. After we fail, we are often afraid to stand before God. But within Deity there exists, as a person, a mercy that knows and embraces our weakness. In the local universe we meet this mercy concretely through the ministry of Michael, that is, Jesus, and his consort, the Creative Spirit (see Paper 33). The way Jesus treated sinners and the sick is the very mercy of the Eternal Son clothed in a human face.

We too must learn this mercy. At home, at work, and in our communities we meet the shortcomings of others every day. If our response then is understanding and help rather than blame and judgment, we are putting the Father's love into action. Mercy does not mean overlooking wrong; it means standing beside the one who did wrong so that he can rise again. It does not abandon justice but completes justice with love. One who shows mercy does not define another by his worst moment but looks upon the best he can become. As the Father sees us in that way, so we must see one another.

Today, I invite you not to keep love only in your heart but to carry it into small acts of mercy. A warm word to someone weary, a hand that helps a colleague set things right after a mistake instead of blaming him, a hand of reconciliation offered first to someone you have long felt hurt by: all of these are applied love. God is love and the Son is mercy; so our lives, as we grow to resemble them, must become a place where love and mercy meet.
d013.pr: Today, once, offer someone who has made a mistake or is weary a concrete helping hand instead of judgment.

msg: The final section of Paper 6 deals with how we may come to comprehend the Eternal Son. This passage begins with a remarkable paradox. The Eternal Son is infinite, yet he is approachable through the persons of his Paradise Sons and through the patient ministry of the Infinite Spirit. The Infinite One has himself prepared a way by which he can reach us in our finiteness.

The text emphasizes this fact from both sides. Without the bestowal service of the Paradise Sons and the loving ministry of the creatures of the Infinite Spirit, beings of material origin could hardly hope to attain the Eternal Son. But it is equally true that, with the help and guidance of these celestial agencies, the God-conscious mortal will certainly attain Paradise. Our ascension is not accomplished by our strength alone; it is achieved surrounded by the love of countless divine beings.

This truth shows the humility and generosity of Deity. God is not one who simply stays on high, waiting for us to climb up on our own. The Sons come down to the lower worlds, even living in the likeness of creatures, while the angels and many other ministers, children of the Infinite Spirit, help us tirelessly at our side. Michael's living as a man on Urantia is the summit of this love (see Paper 120). The ladder to God is one that God first let down to us. Though the height is one we could never climb by our own strength, we can climb it because there are those who come down and take our hand. Our ascension is, from beginning to end, a story of grace and co-operation.

The closing promise of this passage makes the heart swell. The God-conscious mortal will sometime stand in the personal presence of this majestic Son of Sons, the Eternal Son. This is no vague hope but a revealed certainty. Now we are weak beings bound to matter, yet along the path of endless ascension we are destined at last to reach the center of Deity. This destiny is open to all who choose to live in God-consciousness.

This teaching asks of us an attitude of gratitude and co-operation. Knowing that there are beings helping us unseen, we need not wear ourselves out struggling alone. At the same time, we must open our hearts to that help and co-operate with it. Even the finest guide cannot lead one who will not follow. Prayer, meditation, and sincere living are the ways we open ourselves to the spiritual ministry that helps us. When we pray, when a way suddenly opens in the midst of perplexity, when we receive comfort through an unexpected meeting, behind it there may be celestial care we do not fully know. Remembering this deepens our gratitude and humbles our hearts.

Further, we too can become channels through which others draw near to God. Just as the Sons and the angels do for us, the loving service we give our neighbors becomes a window through which they feel God's love. If today I can be someone who helps another feel God a little closer, I am taking part in divine ministry.
d014.pr: Give thanks today for the spiritual ministry that has helped you unseen, and become a channel of God's love to someone.

d015.t: The Spirit Pull upon the Soul
msg: Paper 7 deals with the Eternal Son's relation to the universe, and in particular explains the spirit-gravity circuit. This passage tells us what that circuit means for each of us. The spiritual-gravity pull of the Eternal Son constitutes the inherent secret of the Paradise ascension of surviving human souls. All genuine spirit values and all bona fide spiritualized individuals are held within the unfailing grasp of the spiritual gravity of the Eternal Son.

Just as material gravity draws all physical things toward Paradise, spirit gravity draws all spiritual realities toward the Eternal Son. This pull operates unfailingly, whether or not we feel it. Each time we harbor a true thought, choose a good deed, or open our hearts to God, those spiritual values are caught up in this circuit and preserved as eternal realities. Spiritual values are never scattered into the void. They are held fast by the surest law of the universe.

The text says that the mortal mind initiates its career as a material mechanism and is eventually mustered into the Corps of the Finality as a well-nigh perfected spirit existence. And it explains that during this entire experience the mind becomes progressively less subject to material gravity and correspondingly more responsive to the inward pulling urge of spirit gravity. Our ascension is the process by which our center shifts from the weight of matter to the pull of spirit. That transformation, begun on this earth, continues through the mansion worlds, the local universe, the superuniverse, and Havona (see Paper 14). Not even one small spiritual decision made on earth is lost in the circuits of the universe; each becomes part of the power that lifts us upward.

This truth lets us see our inner life anew. We are often weighed down by the heaviness of material things. Worries about money, health, appearances, and comfort drag our hearts downward. Yet a deeper pull is also at work within us. The longing to know the truth, the desire to do good, the yearning to meet God: these are the very urgings of spirit gravity. The more we respond to that pull, the lighter the weight of matter becomes.

Later in the same section the revelator adds that this circuit responds only to genuine spiritual values. Purely material and self-centered petitions find no place in the spirit-gravity circuit. We must therefore look at the quality of our prayers and desires. We should examine whether what we ask for touches eternal values or remains with passing desires. When we ask for spiritual things, we enter the surest channel of response in the universe. As the content of our prayers matures spiritually, we ask less that God give us things and more that he make us more like him. Such prayers are always answered, and the answer appears as a change in our character.

I invite you today to distinguish between what drags your heart downward and what lifts it upward. Then consciously entrust your heart to what draws it upward. The spirit-gravity circuit literally pulls the soul of man Paradiseward. Our part is not to resist that pull but to respond to it willingly. As those responses accumulate, our souls rise little by little toward the Father's house.
d015.pr: Today, lay down one material worry that weighs on your heart, and in its place pray for one eternal value.

msg: The fifth section of Paper 7 deals with the spirit of bestowal. The Eternal Son unreservedly joined with the Father in the plan for all creatures, and that spirit has passed on to all the Sons who come from him. This passage says that the Eternal Son is the exemplary inspiration for all the Sons of God in their ministrations of bestowal throughout the universes of time and space. The Creator Sons, the Magisterial Sons, and other unrevealed orders of sonship all partake of this wonderful willingness to bestow themselves upon creatures.

Bestowal is not simply giving something away; it is giving oneself. The Sons of God do not merely issue commands from on high; they enter directly into the life of creatures and live in their very likeness. They personally experience the limitations, sufferings, and temptations of creatures, and in the midst of them they show what a life that follows the Father's will looks like. This is the most beautiful humility of Deity and at the same time the deepest expression of love.

The text adds an astonishing truth: in the bestowal of each Son of God upon the worlds of space, in and through and by these bestowals, the Eternal Son has bestowed himself upon the intelligent will creatures of the universes. So when Michael lived as Jesus on Urantia, it was not only the act of one Creator Son; it was an event revealing the bestowal spirit of the Eternal Son himself (see Paper 120). Through the life of Jesus we behold the spirit of self-giving at the very center of Deity. His life is the surest proof that God is not one who watches from afar but one who comes to our side and lives with us.

This teaching shows us what true greatness is. The world regards greatness as rising high and ruling over many. But by the divine standard, greatness lies in coming down to serve. Jesus said that he came not to be served but to serve. The spirit of bestowal shown by the Sons of God testifies to the truth that the higher a being is in the universe, the more willingly he humbles himself.

We too are called to share in this spirit of bestowal. We cannot take on flesh for a world as a Creator Son does, but we can give ourselves where we are. Giving our time to listen to someone lonely, giving our talents to help someone in need, giving our hearts to share another's burden: all these are small bestowals. When we give ourselves in this way, we become one with the spirit of the Eternal Son. Giving is not loss; it is the language of love. When we give ourselves, not only those who receive but we who give grow together, and in the process the shell of selfishness peels away little by little and the soul grows larger.

I invite you today to consider what you have that you could give for the sake of others. Whether it be material things, time, or attention, giving willingly without expecting anything in return is the heart of bestowal. The more we give ourselves, the richer, not the smaller, we become. The path the Sons of God have walked is the path that leads us to the Father.
d016.pr: Today, do one thing in which you willingly give your time or talents for someone else, expecting nothing in return.

msg: Paper 8 introduces the Infinite Spirit, the Third Source and Center, and in its fourth section it explains the Spirit of divine ministry. This passage sums up in a single sentence the distinguishing marks of the three persons of Deity: “⟦Q 8:4.2⟧God is love, the Son is mercy, the Spirit is ministry⟦/Q⟧” — the ministry of divine love and endless mercy to all intelligent creation. The Spirit is the personification of the Father's love and the Son's mercy; in him are they eternally united for universal service.

These three words, love, mercy, and ministry, form a single stream. Love is the source; mercy is that love acting toward beings in their weakness; and ministry is that mercy unfolding in concrete acts of service and help. If love is the spring, mercy is the flowing stream, and ministry is the watering of the parched land. The Infinite Spirit is that watering hand, caring for, comforting, and guiding creatures in every corner of the universe. That hand makes no distinction between great tasks and small, and it reaches even the creature in the lowliest place.

The text says that the Spirit is love applied to the creature creation, the combined love of the Father and the Son. The Creative Spirit we meet in the local universe and her children, the angels and the adjutant mind-spirits, are all expressions of this ministry (see Paper 38). That our minds can think, learn, and worship at all is owing to the ministry of mind that comes from the Infinite Spirit. Even when we are unaware of it, we are constantly receiving the care of this ministry. Behind every moment when we are comforted, gain insight, or find strength to rise again lies the loving care of the Infinite Spirit. We are beings who live surrounded by this ministry.

This truth shows how faith comes to completion in life. If we say we love God but do not serve our neighbors, that love is not yet complete. Love becomes whole only when it passes through mercy and arrives at ministry. Jesus, too, while teaching love for the Father, healed the sick, fed the hungry, and comforted those who mourned. His was a life in which love, mercy, and ministry were joined as one.

We can therefore examine our own spiritual growth by these three stages. We must ask whether we love God and people, whether that love shows itself as mercy toward the weak, and whether that mercy leads on into practical service. If we are stalled at any one stage, we must open our hearts to move on to the next. Service is the final evidence of love and its surest fruit. A faith that confesses love only in words soon withers, but a faith that flows into service is renewed day by day. In the hands that serve, we both convey God's love and come to experience that love more deeply.

I invite you today to practice some small service, following the ministry of the Infinite Spirit. It need not be anything grand. Quietly lightening the load for your family, showing kindness to a stranger, attending to the needs of a neighbor in difficulty: all are ways of sharing in divine ministry. When love becomes mercy and mercy becomes ministry, our lives become a mirror reflecting the character of the Trinity God.
d017.pr: Today, turn the love in your heart into one concrete act of service, and actually lighten the burden of someone close to you.

msg: The last section of Paper 8 deals with the personality of the Infinite Spirit. Because the Infinite Spirit ministers so pervasively throughout the universe, people easily think of him merely as an impersonal force or influence. This passage corrects that misunderstanding. “⟦Q 8:6.4⟧The love of the Spirit⟦/Q⟧” is real, as also are his sorrows; therefore “⟦Q 8:6.4⟧Grieve not the Spirit of God.⟦/Q⟧” The Conjoint Creator is not only the Third Source and Center but also a divine person.

To be a person means to be one who can love, who can rejoice, and who can also grieve. That the Infinite Spirit is a person means that he is not a mechanical force indifferent to our choices and our lives, but one who enters into relationship with us and responds to us. When we follow the truth he rejoices, and when we deliberately reject the light he grieves. This fact lifts our inner life into the dimension of a deep personal relationship. We are therefore invited to treat the Spirit not as a force but as a person, and to share intimate fellowship with him.

The text says that the Spirit speaks to us, makes intercession for us, and exerts a direct and personal influence upon created beings. And it closes with the words “⟦Q 8:6.4⟧For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God.⟦/Q⟧” In the local universe we receive this Spirit's ministry through the Creative Spirit, the Universe Mother Spirit, and her influence reaches into the deepest places of our minds (see Paper 34). We are beings who live in conversation with the Spirit. Because the Spirit makes intercession for us, even when we cannot find the words to pray, he conveys our hearts to the Father. This is Deity's deep consideration for us.

The words “⟦Q 8:6.4⟧He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says⟦/Q⟧” call us to listen. The Spirit does not compel us with a loud voice; he speaks quietly, as in a whisper, to our conscience and our hearts. In our busy and noisy lives we easily miss that voice. To be led by the Spirit, therefore, we need times when we quiet our hearts and listen. Prayer and meditation lower the noise of our minds so that we can hear what the Spirit says.

What does it mean to grieve the Spirit? It is the attitude of turning away from what we know to be right, closing our hearts when we ought to love, and growing stubborn before the truth. To gladden the Spirit, on the other hand, is to respond honestly to the light we have received. It is not great achievements but small obediences that gladden the Spirit. The Spirit waits not for our perfection but for our sincere response. Even when we realize we have grieved the Spirit, there is no need to despair. The moment we turn and face the light again, the Spirit gladly welcomes us and leads us once more. Repentance is the quickest way to restore our relationship with the Spirit.

I invite you today to listen for the small voice of the Spirit within you. The feeling that you should apologize to someone, the prompting to look after one who needs help, the voice of conscience telling you to speak honestly: any of these may be that voice. When we follow its leading, we gladden the Spirit instead of grieving him, and day by day we reaffirm our identity as sons and daughters of God.
d018.pr: Today, do not put off the one thing your conscience is quietly telling you; follow it and act on it.

msg: Paper 9 deals with the relation of the Infinite Spirit to the universe, and in its fifth section it explains the ministry of mind. The Infinite Spirit is the source of all mind, and our capacity to think, judge, and learn is his gift. These two paragraphs honestly show the state in which that divine gift, the mind, exists within us. Mind, on Urantia, is a compromise between the essence of thought perfection and the evolving mentality of our immature human nature. Mind is of divine origin and has a divine destiny, but our mortal minds are not yet of divine dignity.

The paragraph that follows is even more direct. Too often, all too often, we mar our minds by insincerity and sear them with unrighteousness; we subject them to animal fear and distort them by useless anxiety. The revelator describes this almost as a rebuke, but beneath it lies a note of sorrow: sorrow that we ourselves are clouding a precious gift that came from heaven. The fact that the source of mind is divine makes our responsibility all the heavier. Because the mind is a gift received from the Infinite Spirit, how we use it becomes our response to the One who gave it.

The four things pointed out here, insincerity, unrighteousness, fear, and anxiety, are a mirror held up to our inner lives today. Insincerity clouds the clarity of the mind with untrue thoughts and words. Unrighteousness warps the mind with unfair judgments. Fear shrinks the mind so that it cannot look toward higher things, and anxiety drains its strength with useless imaginings. All four are obstacles that block the leading of the spirit (see Paper 100).

The revelator concludes that the contemplation of the immature and inactive human intellect should lead only to reactions of humility. We are quick to take pride in our intellect. But seen from the universe point of view, our minds are still at the very beginning. This humility is not self-contempt but honest self-knowledge. And such knowledge leads us to a teachable spirit, an attitude of opening ourselves to higher mind.

How, then, can we keep the mind pure? First, we must recover sincerity. When we are honest before ourselves and before God, the mind grows clear. Next, we must cultivate the trust that commits our fears and anxieties to the Father. Jesus told us not to be anxious about tomorrow, and to consider the lilies of the field. A mind that trusts God is released from fear and anxiety and regains its native strength. And above all, we must open our minds to the leading of the Adjuster and fill our thoughts with spiritual values. As the mind is purified, the Adjuster's leading is heard more clearly, our judgments become wiser, and our view of our neighbors grows more generous. A pure mind is the best field for the spirit to work in.

I invite you today to look at what is clouding your mind. If there are small lies, unfair judgments, groundless fears, or endless worries, offer them one by one to the Father. Our minds, which are of divine origin, can move forward vigorously toward their divine destiny when they are cultivated in purity. Caring for the mind is the beginning of caring for the soul.
d019.pr: Today, write on paper one worry that weighs on your mind, and lay it down with a prayer committing it to the Father.

msg: The sixth section of Paper 9 explains the mind-gravity circuit. Material gravity acts on matter, spirit gravity on spirit, and mind gravity on mind. Yet this passage emphasizes another reality distinct from all these gravities. Selfhood of personality dignity, human or divine, immortal or potentially immortal, does not originate in either spirit, mind, or matter; it is the bestowal of the Universal Father.

This truth illuminates the deepest mystery of human existence. We have a body, we have a mind, and within us a spirit dwells. Yet the personality that makes me who I am arises from none of these three. It is a unique gift given directly by the Father. The Foreword, too, says that personality is neither body, mind, spirit, nor soul, but the changeless reality that unifies them all (see the Foreword). My personality is the Father's handiwork, the only one of its kind in the whole universe. Personality, therefore, is neither a product of evolution nor a result of environment, but the fruit of a divine act decided by the Father in love. One who knows this comes to look upon the source of his existence with gratitude.

The text says that the operation of personality gravity is always a volitional act of the Universal Father. The Father holds every personality in his personality circuit and through that circuit draws every personality to himself. This is not a mechanical law but a volitional act flowing from the Father's love. Each one of us is directly connected with the Father. No intermediary can sever this connection, and our personality is always within the Father's attention.

This fact is the firmest foundation of human dignity. A person's worth does not come from his abilities, achievements, or social standing. It comes from the fact that he is a being who has received personality as a gift from the Father. Whether intelligent or not, healthy or sick, successful or failing, every personality is equally honorable in being the Father's gift. One who knows this truth cannot treat anyone carelessly.

This teaching also corrects the way we look at ourselves. We often compare ourselves with others and fall into feelings of inferiority or superiority. But my personality is not something to be compared; it is a unique being whom the Father specially intended. The Father made me because he did not want another being exactly like me. When we accept this, we are grateful for ourselves just as we are, and we gain strength to cultivate our personalities according to the Father's will. To belittle another is to make light of the Father who gave him personality; to respect him is to treasure the Father's gift. Brotherly love flows naturally from this realization.

I invite you today to look upon yourself in the mirror, and upon the people you meet, as the Father's gifts. This personality that makes me who I am was given by the Father with eternity in view, and it will survive forever if I choose the will of God. The fitting response of those who have received the gift of personality is gratitude, and the love that gives ourselves to the One who gave the gift.
d020.pr: Today, look upon one person you meet as a unique personality given directly by the Father, and respect that person sincerely.

msg: Paper 10 deals with the Paradise Trinity, and in its first section it explains the self-distribution of the First Source and Center. This passage reveals the essence of divine personality in a single sentence: divine personality is not self-centered; self-distribution and sharing of personality characterize divine freewill selfhood. The Father did not keep himself to himself but chose to share, and that choice is the very nature of divinity.

The text shows that this sharing is a principle flowing through the whole universe. Creatures crave association with other personal creatures, and Creators are moved to share divinity with their universe children. The personality of the Infinite is disclosed as the Universal Father, who shares reality of being and equality of self with the Eternal Son and the Conjoint Actor. The Trinity itself springs from the Father's sharing love. By sharing his infinite self with two co-ordinate personalities, the Father brought about an eternal fellowship. The Trinity reveals not an isolated God but God in eternal communion, and at the source of that communion is the Father's sharing love.

This truth continues in what the Father does for us. The Father has sent a part of himself, the Thought Adjuster, to each of us, and he has given personality as a gift to every person. Earlier in the same section the revelator says that the Father has given away everything he could give. At the center of divinity there is sharing rather than possession, giving rather than grasping. To become like God means to become like this spirit of sharing. Sharing is not an ornament of divinity but its very core. We should remember that the first thing the Father did, before anything else, was to share himself.

This teaching questions the very direction of our lives. We often put ourselves at the center and try to draw everything to ourselves. But self-centeredness is the exact opposite of the mark of divine personality. The more we shut ourselves up within ourselves, the farther we are from God; the more we share ourselves, the nearer we come to God. Personality does not diminish when it is shared; rather, it grows and becomes richer. Love is the one treasure that grows larger the more it is shared.

The words that creatures crave association with other personalities are also worth taking to heart. The longing for fellowship within us, the desire to be understood and to be together, is by no means a weakness. It is a reflection of the divine nature the Father has planted within us. Yet that longing is fulfilled not when we seek only to receive, but when we give and receive in turn. True fellowship comes about when each opens and shares himself. A life lived only for oneself ends up narrow and lonely, but a life of sharing grows ever wider and richer. The words that divine personality is not self-centered are a signpost pointing to what kind of people we ought to become.

May today be a day of sharing what you have. Share not only material things but time, attention, knowledge, and joy. When we open the hearts that wanted to keep things to ourselves and share with our families and neighbors, we take part in the sharing love of the Trinity God. When we share, we come nearest to what is most divine.
d021.pr: Today, gladly share with someone close to you a joy or a lesson you have kept to yourself.

msg: The seventh section of Paper 10 deals with the overcontrol of supremacy, explaining how the Trinity's actions on behalf of the whole universe differ from the individual's point of view. This passage offers us words both honest and comforting. As a son of God you can discern the personal attitude of love in all the acts of God the Father. But you will not always be able to understand how many of the universe acts of the Paradise Trinity redound to the good of the individual mortal.

Two dimensions are distinguished here. One is the Father's personal love. The Father loves each of us as his child, and that love can be discerned in our lives. The other is the universe action of the Trinity. The Trinity works in justice and order for the good not of the individual but of the whole universe. Its acts are so vast and wide that from one person's narrow field of vision their meaning does not always appear clearly. Because we see only one part of the great picture, we easily make the mistake of judging the whole by the part. But the One who sees the whole is guiding all things toward good.

The text says that in the progress of eternity the acts of the Trinity will be revealed as altogether meaningful and considerate, but they do not always so appear to the creatures of time. These words are a promise that what we do not now understand is never meaningless. Now we see through a glass, darkly, but from the vantage of eternity everything will find its place (see Paper 118). Time sees the part; eternity sees the whole. The Father's love is directed to the individual and the Trinity's justice to the whole, yet the two ways meet at last in the same good purpose.

This teaching is a special source of strength in seasons of suffering and confusion. When something incomprehensible befalls us, we ask God why. That question itself is honest and precious. But we cannot obtain an answer to every question right away. At such times we can hold on to two things: the assurance that the Father's personal love never changes, and the trust that the meaning we cannot now see will one day be revealed.

Mature faith is not a faith that understands everything but a faith that trusts even in the midst of not understanding. A small child believes in his parents' love even without understanding all their decisions. We too do not know all the Father's ways, but we can know his love. When we lean on that love and humbly accept the limits of our understanding, our hearts escape the whirlpool of doubt and find peace. Trust is not ignorant resignation but a peace that comes from knowing the character of the One we love. The better we know the Father, the more willingly we can entrust ourselves to him, even without understanding all his ways.

If there is something in your life today that you cannot understand, I invite you to place it in the Father's hands rather than straining to explain it. And look, even there, for the traces of the Father's love that can be discerned. The day will come when, in the light of eternity, all things will be revealed as meaningful. Until that day we walk on, step by step, trusting in love.
d022.pr: Entrust to the Father one thing that troubles you because you cannot understand it, and look for the traces of love you can find in it.

d023.t: All Paths Lead to the Father
msg: Paper 11 describes the eternal Isle of Paradise, and in its first section it reveals that Paradise is the divine residence. This passage says that every path in the universe finally converges on one place. Whether we trace the personality circuit back through the universes, trace the lines of material gravity, follow the lines of spiritual gravity, trace out the mind circuits, or follow the processional of the Sons of God and the celestial beings, all these observations lead us directly back to the Father's presence, to his central abode.

This description shows that the very structure of the universe embodies spiritual truth. The material world, the world of mind, and the world of spirit are all arranged in order toward the same center. The universe is not a collection of things scattered by chance but one vast family woven together around the Father. The courses of the stars, the currents of thought, and the longings of the spirit all incline toward that center. In this unity we realize that the universe is the Father's house. This order tells us that we are not beings abandoned in chaos, but beings held in the Father's embrace from beginning to end.

The text emphasizes that here God is personally, literally, and actually present. God is everywhere by his spirit, yet at the same time he dwells personally on Paradise. And from his infinite being there flow the flood-streams of life, energy, and personality to all universes. The Father is at once the center that draws all things in and the source from which all things flow out. Receiving and giving are one in him (see Paper 5). Because he is not a distant concept but a person who actually dwells there, we can actually journey toward him.

This truth illuminates the direction of our lives. Our lives, too, have many paths: the path of study, the path of work, the path of relationships, the path of suffering. Yet if we walk any of these paths sincerely, they lead at last to the Father. The scientist who honestly searches for truth, the artist who pursues beauty, and the ordinary person who serves his neighbors all meet the same Father at the end of their paths. Every sincere search is a search for the Father.

At the same time, this passage tells us where we draw our life and energy. The streams of life flowing from the Father are reaching us even at this moment. When we are weary and parched, we can gain new strength by returning to that source and opening our hearts. Worship and prayer reconnect us to those streams. A life joined to its source never runs dry. All who live sincerely are walking the road to the Father without knowing it. We should therefore not be quick to judge those who walk different paths, but regard them as fellow pilgrims bound for the same center.

I invite you today to consider where the path you are walking is headed. And resolve in your heart that the work you do and the relationships you form will become part of a pilgrimage toward the Father. As all the paths of the universe converge on the Father, so when every moment of our lives converges on him, we become people with a center that is never scattered.
d023.pr: Today, regard one task you do as a step on the path to the Father, and do it with all your heart.

msg: After describing at length the structure and functions of Paradise, Paper 11 sums up in its last section what all of it means for us. This passage is its conclusion. After all, to mortals the most important thing about eternal Paradise is the fact that this perfect abode of the Universal Father is the real and far-distant destiny of the immortal souls of the mortal and material sons of God, the ascending creatures of the evolutionary worlds.

Descriptions of Paradise can sometimes feel too remote and difficult. Talk of the structure of space, the centers of force, and the source of gravity seems to have nothing to do with our daily lives. But at the end of all those descriptions the revelator says, in effect: this is where you are going. Before Paradise is a subject of astronomy, it is our destination. The Father's house at the center of the distant universe awaits us, and that fact gives meaning to all our knowledge of Paradise. All knowledge of the universe is ultimately meant to answer the question of where we came from and where we are going, and the answer is the Father's house.

The text goes on to say something even more astonishing: every God-knowing mortal who has espoused the career of doing the Father's will has already embarked upon the long, long Paradise trail of divinity pursuit and perfection attainment. The journey does not begin after death. The moment we choose to do the Father's will, we are already standing on the road to Paradise. Our life today is the first stretch of that journey, never a time of waiting (see Paper 14). This destiny is not open only to a special few; it is open to all who know God and seek to do his will.

The last sentence of this passage is full of wonder. When a being of animal origin, having ascended from the lowly spheres of space, at last stands before the Gods on Paradise, such an achievement represents the reality of a spiritual transformation bordering on the limits of supremacy. A being who began in the clay reaching the center of Deity: a greater transformation is hard to imagine. And the text says that countless numbers have now completed that road. This is not a dream but a reality already coming to pass. This transformation is not a miracle that happens all at once but the result of patient growth through many worlds and many stages. And its first stage is our life here and now on this earth.

This truth gives our lives deep dignity and hope. However small and weak we may feel, we are travelers who have set out on the greatest adventure in the universe. Today's small decisions, small acts of love, and small patience are all steps on that long journey. The traveler who knows his destination does not grow weary even when the road is rough. One who remembers the destination of Paradise does not lose meaning even amid the toils of everyday life.

I invite you to take this fact to heart and begin your day this morning: I am already on the road to the Father's house. This confession lifts our gaze on high and frees us from petty worries. The road is long, but the Father waits at its end, the Adjuster walks with us, and multitudes have walked that road before us. We too gladly join their procession.
d024.pr: This morning, confess that you are already on the journey to Paradise, and take the first step of your day.

msg: After describing the vast structure of the universe of universes, Paper 12 turns in its seventh section to the relation of part and whole. How small is one individual in so vast a universe? This passage gives a wonderful answer. The love of the Father absolutely individualizes each personality as a unique child of the Universal Father, a child without duplicate in infinity, a will creature irreplaceable in all eternity. However great the universe may be, a single person within it is never lost from view.

We live in an age of numbers and statistics. People are easily treated as a figure, a function, a part that can be replaced at any time. At work and in society alike we often feel that we are replaceable. But in the Father's eyes we are never such beings. Search the whole infinite universe and there is no one exactly like me; until eternity ends there is no one who can take my place. The Father loves me, precisely me and no one else. To him we are not one among countless multitudes but children called by name.

The text says that the Father's love glorifies each child of God, illuminating each member of the celestial family. That love sharply silhouettes the unique nature of each personal being and strikingly portrays the transcendent value of each will creature. The Father's love is not a love that dissolves us into the crowd; rather, it is a love that makes the uniqueness of each of us shine more clearly. The more we are loved, the more we become ourselves. This is the firmest foundation of our existence.

This passage also makes plain the reach of that love. From the highest creator personality of Paradise status to the lowest personality of will dignity among the savage tribes of men in the dawn of the human species on some evolutionary world, the Father places a high value upon each and every one of his children. High and low cannot divide his love. This is the core truth of the same section, which teaches the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man (see Paper 194). Because all people are irreplaceable children of the same Father, we are all brothers and sisters. This realization heals both inferiority and pride, establishing us as people who are at once humble and assured.

This truth builds up our self-worth at the very deepest level. Self-worth that comes from the approval of others or from worldly success is easily shaken. But the fact that the Father loves me as his irreplaceable child does not change in any circumstance. Even on the day I fail, even on the day I am rejected, I am still the Father's one and only child. One who stands on this assurance is not swayed by the judgments of others and is free to love.

And this truth also changes how we treat others. If I am irreplaceable, then the person before me is just as irreplaceable. To treat him carelessly or use him as a tool is to make light of a being whom the Father holds infinitely precious. I invite you to look upon each person you meet today as a child of the Father without duplicate in infinity. That way of seeing makes our relationships holy.
d025.pr: Today, look in the mirror and say, "I am the Father's irreplaceable child," and look upon those you meet in the same way.
